title: Creating Line, Bar and Scatter Charts
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Creating Line, Bar and Scatter Charts.
Select appropriate Python library operations for the analytical question.
Inspect inputs, data types and intermediate results before interpreting output.
Validate calculations and communicate results with suitable evidence.
Identify assumptions, edge cases and limitations in the analysis.

understand.concept: Chart type should match the analytical question. Line charts show ordered trends, bar charts compare discrete categories, and scatter plots show relationships between two numeric variables. The choice of axes, scales, aggregation and sampling can change interpretation. Avoid connecting unordered categories with lines or using bars when a continuous relationship is the focus.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable data analysis requires choosing operations that match the question and checking how transformations affect the evidence. Clear methods make results easier to reproduce, explain and review.
understand.analogy: Think of an analysis as preparing a carefully labeled report: organize the records, calculate the measures, and present the evidence. The analogy is limited because real data requires explicit validation and statistical judgment.
understand.summary: Creating Line, Bar and Scatter Charts extends the Python data-analysis workflow with practical, reproducible techniques.

explain.narrative: Prepare and validate the values before plotting. Use line charts for time or another meaningful sequence, bars for category comparisons, and scatter plots for paired numeric observations. Label units, keep category ordering intentional, and inspect outliers and overlapping points. A visual pattern is descriptive evidence, not proof of a mechanism.

examples.title: Draw a line chart
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 7], marker='o')
print(len(ax.lines))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A line chart connects values in a meaningful order, such as time.

examples.title: Compare categories with bars
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(['A', 'B', 'C'], [3, 5, 2])
print(len(ax.patches))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Each category is represented by a separate rectangular bar.

examples.title: Plot paired numeric values
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
print(len(ax.collections))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: scatter adds a collection of points and helps inspect relationships between numeric variables.

examples.title: Set an explicit category order
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], [2, 5, 8])
print([tick.get_text() for tick in ax.get_xticklabels()])
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Passing categories in a deliberate order prevents accidental alphabetical or data-order interpretation.

examples.title: Compare chart artist counts
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].plot([1, 2], [2, 3])
axes[1].bar(['X', 'Y'], [4, 6])
print(len(axes[0].lines), len(axes[1].patches))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Different Axes can show different views of the same dataset.

practise.guidedTask: Use one prepared dataset to create a line chart of monthly revenue, a bar chart of revenue by category and a scatter plot of advertising spend against revenue. Label all axes and explain why each chart type fits its question.
practise.independentTask: Choose chart types for five business questions and justify the mapping from question to chart, including any aggregation or ordering required.
hints: Use line charts only when x has a meaningful order.
Use bars to compare discrete categories.
Use scatter for two numeric variables.
Set category order explicitly when it carries meaning.
practise.challenge: Create a three-panel figure that presents a trend, category comparison and numeric relationship from a shared dataset without changing the source DataFrame.
